Single-stage impulse oxygen turbine

26 kg/s of oxygen expanding from 220 bar and 700 K to 140 bar, at 30000 rpm. The grey row is the nozzle vanes, the red row the rotor blades. The rotor is shrouded, so the casing over it turns with it. The translucent surfaces are the hub and casing. Rotate and zoom to look at the blades.

A pressure ratio of about 1.57 across 700 K oxygen gives a spouting velocity of about 400 m/s. One impulse stage takes it at a blade-to-jet ratio of 0.45, near where an impulse stage works best, which at 30 000 rpm puts the mean diameter at about 116 mm.

At zero reaction the nozzle takes the whole static enthalpy drop: the flow leaves it at Mach 0.74, almost tangentially. The rotor turns the flow back through about 135° at constant relative speed, and it leaves nearly axially. The rotor still loses some static pressure, because half the stage's losses are charged to it.

The meanline runs at one mean radius. Blade heights follow from continuity at each station's density. That density comes from the station's enthalpy and the entropy the supplied efficiency implies, shared evenly between the two rows.

Metal angles, stagger and chord are the drawing's values at mean radius. Pitch, throat and gauging angle are measured on the built mid-span section. The gauging angle, acos(throat/pitch), is roughly where the flow leaves each row, so its distance from the outlet metal angle shows how the drawn blade differs from the triangles it was drawn for.

Stagger decides most of that distance. The nozzle turns the flow to nearly 80°, and its chord leans 80 % of the way to the outlet angle (stagger_fraction=0.8) to bring its gauging angle within about 2°. The rotor is a symmetric impulse blade (SectionProfile.impulse), with its chord just past the mean of its metal angles.

Does the flow choke? Mach numbers are absolute for the nozzle and relative for the rotor. Areas are per blade passage: gap times blade height, taken where the gap is. Sonic area is how small the passage could get before the flow entering it reached Mach 1: the inlet area over the ideal-gas A/A* at the inlet Mach number, with γ from CoolProp at the row inlet. The smallest area stays above it in both rows, so neither chokes. This is a one-dimensional, loss-free estimate at mid-span; losses shrink the margin a little. The nozzle comes closest, since it is meant to accelerate its flow to Mach 0.74. The rotor, at a relative Mach of about 0.4, has room to spare. A pinch of one means the passage narrows no further than the smaller of its inlet width and throat.

Free-vortex twist: the rotor twists more than the nozzle, since blade speed grows with radius.
